turns.prompt_text: I'm using a 3D printer, Bamboo Studio. I have some small pieces I would like to print, but I want them solid all the way through. These are going to hold a belt, so they need to be structurally tight. Right now, the infill is set to grid.
turns.response_html:
To make your pieces completely solid in Bambu Studio, you just need to adjust a couple of settings in the Strength tab. However, because these parts need to hold a belt and handle structural tension, how you make them solid matters just as much as the density itself.

Here is exactly how to configure your settings for maximum strength.

The Engineering Nuance: Walls vs. Infill

If your parts are handling tension from a belt (similar to the mechanical stress on a winch or gear), wall loops actually provide significantly more structural strength than 100% infill.

When you slice a model with 100% infill, the internal plastic is laid down in short, back-and-forth segments. When you increase your Wall loops (also found in the Strength tab), the printer lays down continuous, unbroken strands of filament that trace the perimeter of your part.

Continuous strands are much harder to break under tension than the small, fused segments of standard infill.

For the strongest possible part on your A1: Instead of just relying on 100% infill, try increasing your Wall loops to 6, 8, or even 10 (until the walls meet in the middle of the part), and setting your infill to something like 40-50% Gyroid to fill any remaining tiny gaps. This creates a part that is essentially solid, prints cleaner, and handles mechanical stress much better.

turns.prompt_text: How does the orientation of a 3D print on the build plate affect its mechanical strength?
turns.response_html:
Because 3D printers build parts one horizontal layer at a time, the finished print acts a lot like a piece of wood: it has a "grain."

In engineering terms, FDM 3D printing is anisotropic—meaning its physical strength changes depending on the direction the force is applied.

The X/Y Axis vs. The Z Axis

When your nozzle lays down a single layer of plastic (the X and Y axes), it is extruding a continuous, unbroken strand of material. Pulling on that continuous strand requires a lot of force to break it.

However, the bond between the stacked layers (the Z axis) is just melted plastic squished onto slightly cooler plastic. This layer-to-layer adhesion is the weakest point of any 3D print. If you apply tension that pulls those layers apart, the part will easily split (delaminate) right along the seam long before the plastic itself actually snaps.

What This Means for Your Belt Setup

Since your pieces are holding a belt under tension, orientation is the single most critical factor for their survival.

You must orient your parts on the Bambu Studio build plate so that the pull of the belt runs parallel to the layer lines.

  • The Wrong Way: If the belt pulls upward against the Z-axis, it will rip the top layers right off your part.
  • The Right Way: Lay the part flat on its side so the tension of the belt pulls across the continuous strands of the X/Y axes. The mechanical stress should fight the continuous plastic paths, not the seams between them.

Sometimes finding the perfect orientation requires a tradeoff—you might need to use more support material to print it sideways, but the massive gain in structural strength is absolutely worth the extra filament and post-processing.
